title: The Day Virgin Atlantic Flew Its Only Plane to Newark
dek: In 1984 Richard Branson took up a lawyer's airline idea over his partners' doubts and launched with one second-hand 747, leased for a year.

story.company: Virgin Atlantic Airways (first proposed as British Atlantic Airways)
story.event: Launching a transatlantic airline with one leased second-hand Boeing 747
story.summary: In February 1984 the American-born lawyer Randolph Fields, owner of the British Atlantic Airways name, approached Richard Branson about a new transatlantic airline; Branson took it up despite objections from his Virgin partners and bankers. Virgin Atlantic flew its first service from Gatwick to Newark on 22 June 1984 with its only aircraft, a second-hand Boeing 747 leased from Boeing for a year. Fields later left with a settlement that included free first-class travel for life.
paragraphs: On Friday 22 June 1984, a Boeing 747 called Maiden Voyager left Gatwick for Newark about 25 minutes late. It was the only aircraft Virgin Atlantic had: a second-hand 747-200, formerly flown by Aerolíneas Argentinas. The day before, a BBC reporter on board later wrote, it had needed an unscheduled engine change. On the upper deck the party had already started.

A few months earlier the airline did not exist. In February 1984 Randolph Fields, an American-born lawyer who owned the name British Atlantic Airways, approached Richard Branson, then known for records and shops, about investing in a new transatlantic carrier. Branson's partners at Virgin objected and his bankers were unenthusiastic. Laker Airways, the cut-price transatlantic carrier run by Branson's hero Freddie Laker, had collapsed only two years before. Branson was intrigued at once. In his own retellings the airline begins with a phone call to Boeing, which, he has said, agreed to lease him a second-hand 747 for a year while he tried to get the business going.

Laker gave him advice: sell a business cabin as well as economy, so that bigger rivals could not simply beat Virgin on price. Fields had first proposed business class only, and Branson had wanted low fares; the airline launched with both. On the first flight, Branson later recalled, he sat with Joan, later his wife, and their daughter Holly, watched the crew smiling and joking, and wondered whether the airline would last more than three or four years. When he got home to west London, he said, the bank manager was sitting on his doorstep.

The partnership did not last. Fields left Virgin with a settlement that, his obituary in The Herald said, included free first-class travel for life for himself, two friends and his mother. In 1987 he tried again with Highland Express, flying one jumbo jet between Prestwick and New York, and lost more than £1 million. He died in 1997, aged 44. Maiden Voyager stayed with Virgin Atlantic until 2001, and by 2020 thirty 747s had flown in its fleet.

quote.text: And make the counsel of thy heart to stand; for there is none more faithful unto thee than it. For a man’s soul is sometime wont to bring him tidings, more than seven watchmen that sit on high on a watch-tower.
quote.translator: Revised Version of the Apocrypha (1895), as selected in the Wisdom of the East series (1910)
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira advises letting the counsel of your own heart stand, because it can sometimes see further than seven watchmen on a tower. Branson's partners and bankers were the watchmen. He went with his own reading, and kept the first step to one plane and a one-year lease.

reflection: Most tellings give the credit to Branson's instinct, but notice what sat underneath it: one aircraft, a lease for a year, and a cabin designed so the airline could not be beaten on price alone. He trusted himself and still made the cost of being wrong survivable.

You will have days when the people around you see only the risk, and sometimes they will be right. Your own judgement deserves a hearing as well, especially about work you know closely. It is easier to give it one once you have also decided how small a first step can be.
invitation: Take one idea you keep talking yourself out of. Write down the smallest version you could try for a month, and what it would cost you if it failed. Then leave it there for today.

research_notes: Origin story: Branson's own retellings (CNBC 2019; Virgin Atlantic's 747 farewell page) begin with his phone call to Boeing, and CNBC links that call to his hiring a plane after a cancelled flight to the Virgin Islands, undated, without mentioning Fields. The Gale biography and John Bell's BTN account say Fields brought the idea to Branson in February or early 1984. The story gives both, attributing the Boeing call to Branson. Fields's original concept: Gale says an all-business-class airline; BTN (22 June 2020) says the British Atlantic idea was to fly to the Falkland Islands; the story uses only Gale's version, set against the two-class cabin Branson launched with on Laker's advice (Independent 2024). Lease terms: CNBC reports a one-year lease; Branson elsewhere (his virgin.com blog, which blocks automated requests) says Boeing would consider taking the plane back after a year; the story says only that it was leased for a year. Engine: Bell recalls an unscheduled engine change the day before the first flight; the bird-strike episode told in Branson's memoir could not be confirmed in a loadable source and is left out. Fields's exit: The Herald describes a severance settlement of lifetime first-class travel for him, two friends and his mother; David Spanier in The Independent says he sold his share in return for lifetime free first-class travel; Wikipedia gives £125,000 compensation in September 1984 and a £1m buyout in 1985, which I could not confirm in a loadable source, so the story names only the free-travel element and gives no date for his departure. The Herald's line that Highland Express showed one jumbo jet is not enough is the paper's judgement and is not repeated as fact; its note about an inaugural flight delayed by refurbishment refers to Highland Express, not Virgin. The Independent 2024 interview is also syndicated on AOL. Funding is 'mixed': Virgin's own money, a lease from Boeing and bank credit; no source gives the start-up sum. The Ben Sira text follows the Revised Version (1895) as printed in the 1910 Wisdom of the East selection, which carries no verse numbers; 37:13-14 is the usual numbering.
